title: Lines that support autonomy
statement: Write what a lesson's guide says to listen, offer hints, encourage and acknowledge the learner's view, and leave out directives, 'you should' statements and handed-over answers.
example: In a lab study, eight behaviours, offering hints among them, predicted higher perceived autonomy, and six, directives among them, predicted lower.
detail: The Grade 9 research brief read in full a lab study of one-on-one sessions: listening, letting the student work their own way, student talk time, informational praise, encouragement, offering hints, answering the student's questions and acknowledging their perspective predicted higher perceived autonomy, while holding onto the materials, showing or saying the answers, directives, 'should / got to' statements and controlling questions predicted lower. The brief uses it as a style guide for the guide's lines and the model's prompts and bans 'you need to / you should / tap here', and the Grade 9 strategy adopts it as its line-writing guide.
against: The study was correlational, in a lab, with adult participants in a 10-minute one-on-one session (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/learners-voice-guide.md`, line 41). Its supportive list includes informational praise, which the lesson engine's plain-voice rule bans from every line a student reads.

evidence.quote: Eight behaviors predicted higher perceived autonomy: listening, letting the student work their own way, time the student spends talking, informational praise, encouragement, offering hints, answering student questions, and acknowledging the student's perspective.
Six predicted lower autonomy: holding onto the materials, showing or saying the answers, directives, "should / got to" statements, and controlling questions.
Ban "you need to / you should / tap here."
